extracted.intended_audience: general readers and students of philosophy/literature (readers of Montaigne)
extracted.subtask_description: Close-reading / interpretation of Montaigne's Essays (selected chapters) addressing human conduct, death, desire, and reputation; the page is a translated excerpt exploring norms and observations about suicide, indecision, desire, and glory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer a short, least-premeditated death
rubrics_metrics.description: A short and least premeditated death is the most desirable end; Caesar said he preferred "the least premeditated and the shortest," and Pliny called a short death "the sovereign good hap of human life."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid prolonged dying and over-elaboration: long, drawn-out deaths give time for reflection, repentance, and suffering; examples: Caesar's maxim, the Stoic admiration of promptness in death, contrasted with tortures that 'make men feel death.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Elaborate preparations indicate effeminacy or lack of true resolve
rubrics_metrics.description: Lavish or theatrical preparations for suicide (e.g., Heliogabalus' golden cords, emerald poisons, ornate methods) betray effeminacy and suggest the person would likely change their mind when actually forced to die.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne treats ostentatious arrangements for self-killing as signs one has not really resolved to die; the more one plans death as ceremony, the less likely one truly is to follow through when tested.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constancy (decisive single action) is required for a genuine suicide
rubrics_metrics.description: True resolution in taking one's life requires firmness and a decisive act (a single effective blow) rather than lingering or half-measures which allow the sensibility of the body to oppose the will.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical examples show failed or hesitant attempts (Domitius, Pompeian examples); advice is to choose means that do not permit waxing regret or gradual loss of resolve—"a morsel that is to be swallowed without chewing."

rubrics_metrics.name: Leisurely contemplation and digestion of death is noble (Socratic ideal)
rubrics_metrics.description: Socrates’ having thirty days to ruminate on his sentence and meet death calmly is presented as one of the most illustrious examples of facing death with composed reflection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Taking time to reflect and reconcile oneself to death can produce assured hope and tranquility rather than agitation; contrasted with panic or theatrical behaviour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methods of self-destruction by abstinence may both attempt death and restore life
rubrics_metrics.description: Cases where abstinence or fasting was chosen to end life sometimes resulted in recovery (Pomponius Atticus, Cleanthes); the same means used to kill may unexpectedly cure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choosing methods that allow a gradual process can produce unforeseen outcomes (recovery), so such methods bear uncertainty; Montaigne narrates these as paradoxical 'studied and digested deaths.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not unnecessarily involve or endanger others when ending one's life
rubrics_metrics.description: One should avoid making servants or others complicit in one’s death (domestics are suspected, and involvement may render others culpable); leave small legacies to servants to avoid suspicion and console them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Stoic counsel related to Marcellinus: preserve dignity, arrange for dependents so as not to implicate others, and avoid creating scandal or suspicion through the method chosen.

rubrics_metrics.name: The mind cannot be exactly balanced between two indifferent choices
rubrics_metrics.description: It is a pleasant imagination that the soul could be perfectly balanced between two equal desires, but in reality slight differences (perception, touch, chance) always incline choice; true perfect indifference is impossible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stoic explanations that choice arises from accidental impulses are questioned; Montaigne prefers the view that imperceptible differences always exist, so decisions inevitably occur.

rubrics_metrics.name: Desire is heightened by difficulty and scarcity
rubrics_metrics.description: What is forbidden, rare, or difficult becomes more desired; difficulty and hazard increase the pleasure and estimation of things (love, goods, devotion, amusements).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: veils, modesty, and obstacles in love increase attraction; Lycurgus' Spartan decree; satiety follows facility; aphorisms quoted (Seneca, Lucretius). Application extends to social and religious life where opposition can revive zeal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition and liberty have opposite effects on attachment
rubrics_metrics.description: Removing an object from easy possession or forbidding it sharpens appetite; conversely, absolute possession or too much liberty can slacken affection (e.g., Roman divorce liberty preserved marital honour).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institutions that forbid or restrict sometimes strengthen attachment and commitment; too much ease or absolute control can produce satiety or contempt.

rubrics_metrics.name: Excessive defence or ostentation of defence can invite attack
rubrics_metrics.description: Displaying or over-investing in defensive measures gives an enemy both invitation and pretext: openness and lack of showy defence can sometimes preserve peace (Argippians, cotton-fenced fields).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne argues that visible defences may provoke assault and that modesty of defence can deter aggression; over-guarding may also imply improvidence and expose one to blame when taken.

rubrics_metrics.name: Glory is external, accidental, and often vain — not a proper sole motive
rubrics_metrics.description: Glory (the world's approbation) is a name joined to the thing, external and not part of a person's substance; philosophers like Chrysippus and Diogenes counseled contempt of glory because it is dangerous and corrupting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pursuing glory alone leads to flattery, corruption of princes, and hollow motives; Montaigne concedes glory can bring practical benefits, but warns against making virtue depend on public praise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Virtue motivated by reputation is vain; true virtue is internal and act-based
rubrics_metrics.description: If virtue is sought only for honour or reputation, it is vain; true magnanimity judges virtue by deeds rather than by the glory attached to them — concealed virtue little differs from sloth if it serves only as reputation's means.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne and Carneades/Cicero debate whether glory may be desirable for itself, but Montaigne insists virtue should not be regulated by public opinion; examples include the condemnation of actions done only when witnessed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fortune, not merit, often determines public renown
rubrics_metrics.description: Reputation and renown frequently depend on accident and fortune rather than on intrinsic merit; Caesar and Alexander's fame owed much to fortune's favour and survivorship of perils.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many brave deeds die unrecorded; reliance on public recognition is precarious because chance often carries some to greatness while cutting others off; thus seeking glory is unstable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not perform good actions only for witnesses — authenticity matters
rubrics_metrics.description: Instructions that value actions only when celebrated condition people to act for spectators rather than from nature; true goodness exists in the act itself, not in its being seen or celebrated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne criticises teachings that encourage valor only when it will be observed; many noble acts occur unobserved and are no less virtuous — acting for glory corrupts motive and may reduce the substance of virtue.
